slides.title: Human Vectors and Social Engineering
points: Social engineering targets people rather than purely technical weaknesses. Objective 2.2 expects you to distinguish the delivery method, impersonation style, and manipulation technique.
Security+ Objective 2.2: explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.

slides.title: Phishing
slides.teach: Fraudulent messages designed to trick victims into revealing information, opening malicious content, or taking unsafe actions.

course.learn: Fraudulent messages designed to trick victims into revealing information, opening malicious content, or taking unsafe actions.

breakdown.explanation: General message-based social engineering.
Credential phishing email, Fake login link

course.why: Attackers exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity rather than a technical flaw alone.
course.example: A fake Microsoft login email steals user credentials.
course.check_q: What is the broad term for fraudulent messages designed to trick victims?

slides.title: Vishing
slides.teach: Voice-based phishing performed through phone or voice communication.

course.learn: Voice-based phishing performed through phone or voice communication.

breakdown.explanation: Phishing by voice.
Fake bank call, Fake help desk call

course.why: A live caller can create urgency and pressure a victim into revealing information.
course.example: A caller pretends to be the bank fraud department.
course.check_q: What is phishing over the phone called?

slides.title: Smishing
slides.teach: SMS-based phishing delivered through text messages.

course.learn: SMS-based phishing delivered through text messages.

breakdown.explanation: Phishing by text.
Fake package text, Fraudulent bank SMS

course.why: Mobile users may react quickly to urgent text-message lures.
course.example: A fake package-delivery text contains a malicious link.
course.check_q: What is phishing by SMS called?

slides.title: Misinformation / Disinformation
slides.teach: Misinformation is false information shared without necessarily intending deception; disinformation is deliberately false or misleading information spread to deceive.

course.learn: Misinformation is false information shared without necessarily intending deception; disinformation is deliberately false or misleading information spread to deceive.

breakdown.explanation: Both are false information, but disinformation includes deliberate deception.
False rumor, Coordinated false narrative

course.why: False information can manipulate decisions, trust, reputation, or security behavior.
course.example: A coordinated campaign deliberately spreads false claims to manipulate users.
course.exam: Accidental false info = misinformation; deliberate false info = disinformation.
course.check_q: Which term describes deliberately false information spread to deceive?

slides.title: Impersonation
slides.teach: Pretending to be another trusted person or organization.

course.learn: Pretending to be another trusted person or organization.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker pretends to be someone trusted.
Fake executive, Fake IT technician

course.why: Victims may comply because they believe the request comes from a trusted identity.
course.example: An attacker pretends to be the CFO and requests sensitive payroll data.
course.check_q: What technique involves pretending to be a trusted person?

slides.title: Business Email Compromise
slides.teach: Targeted email fraud in which attackers impersonate or compromise business accounts to manipulate payments, data sharing, or business processes.

course.learn: Targeted email fraud in which attackers impersonate or compromise business accounts to manipulate payments, data sharing, or business processes.

breakdown.explanation: Business email is abused to trick employees into financial or sensitive actions.
Fake wire request, Compromised executive mailbox

course.why: BEC exploits normal business workflows and trust in executives, vendors, or finance processes.
course.example: A finance employee receives a fraudulent CEO email requesting an urgent wire transfer.
course.check_q: What attack targets business email workflows to manipulate payments?

slides.title: Pretexting
slides.teach: Creating a believable fabricated story or scenario to persuade a victim to reveal information or perform an action.

course.learn: Creating a believable fabricated story or scenario to persuade a victim to reveal information or perform an action.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker invents a convincing reason for the request.
Fake audit request, Fake HR verification

course.why: A believable story makes an unusual request seem legitimate.
course.example: An attacker claims to be an auditor who urgently needs employee records.
course.check_q: What technique uses a fabricated scenario to justify a request?

slides.title: Watering Hole
slides.teach: Compromising a website frequently visited by a target group so visitors can be attacked.

course.learn: Compromising a website frequently visited by a target group so visitors can be attacked.

breakdown.explanation: Poison the site your targets already visit.
Compromised industry website

course.why: Attackers take advantage of predictable browsing behavior and trust in the site.
course.example: An industry forum is compromised to infect members who visit it.
course.exam: Target's favorite site compromised → WATERING HOLE.
course.check_q: What attack compromises a site frequently visited by the target group?

slides.title: Brand Impersonation
slides.teach: Pretending to represent a trusted brand or company to deceive victims.

course.learn: Pretending to represent a trusted brand or company to deceive victims.

breakdown.explanation: Copy the look and identity of a familiar company.
Fake Microsoft login, Fake bank website

course.why: Recognizable branding lowers suspicion and increases trust.
course.example: A fake bank login page uses the real bank's logo and design.
course.check_q: What technique copies a trusted company's brand identity?

slides.title: Typosquatting
slides.teach: Registering lookalike domains based on common spelling errors or visual similarity.

course.learn: Registering lookalike domains based on common spelling errors or visual similarity.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker creates a domain that looks almost like the real one.
micros0ft.example, paypa1-style domain

course.why: Users may mistype or overlook subtle differences in domain names.
course.example: A user enters a common misspelling of a company domain and lands on a malicious site.
course.check_q: What technique uses misspelled or lookalike domains?

rows: False info without required intent to deceive

blocks.title: Match the social-engineering clue
items: Email/social message → PHISHING
Phishing is the broad message-based social-engineering category.
Example: A fake Microsoft login email steals credentials.
Phone call → VISHING
Vishing is phishing conducted through voice communication.
Example: A caller pretends to be the bank fraud department.
Text message → SMISHING
Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS.
Example: A fake package-delivery text contains a malicious link.
Believable made-up story → PRETEXTING
The attacker invents a scenario to justify the request.
Example: Someone claims to be an auditor who urgently needs employee records.
Executive/vendor payment request → BEC
Business email compromise targets business workflows, especially payments or sensitive data.
Example: A finance employee receives a fake CEO wire-transfer request.
Target's favorite site compromised → WATERING HOLE
Attackers compromise a site the target population already trusts and visits.
Example: An industry forum is infected to target members.
Trusted company's name/logo → BRAND IMPERSONATION
The attacker copies a brand identity to gain trust.
Example: A fake bank login page uses the real bank's logo.
Misspelled lookalike domain → TYPOSQUATTING
The attacker relies on a domain that resembles the legitimate one.
Example: A user types a common misspelling and lands on a malicious site.
blocks.example: Memory: Phishing = message · Vishing = voice · Smishing = SMS · Pretext = story · BEC = business email · Watering hole = trusted site · Brand = fake identity · Typo = fake domain.

questions.q: A fake Microsoft login email asks a user to enter credentials. Which social-engineering technique is this?
questions.explanation: The fraudulent message is a phishing attempt.

questions.q: A caller pretending to be the bank asks for an account verification code. Which technique is this?
A fake package-delivery text contains a malicious link. Which technique is this?
A coordinated campaign deliberately spreads false claims to deceive users. Which term best fits?
questions.explanation: Disinformation is deliberately false or misleading information spread to deceive.

questions.q: An attacker pretends to be the CFO and requests payroll data. Which technique is most directly being used?
questions.explanation: The attacker is pretending to be a trusted individual.

questions.q: A finance employee receives a fake CEO email requesting an urgent wire transfer. Which attack best fits?
questions.explanation: BEC targets business email workflows, often involving payments.

questions.q: An attacker claims to be an auditor and invents a story about an urgent compliance review to obtain records. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Pretexting uses a fabricated scenario to justify the request.

questions.q: Attackers compromise an industry website frequently visited by employees of a target company. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: A watering-hole attack compromises a site the target population already visits.

questions.q: A fake bank website copies the real bank's logo, colors, and design. Which technique is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: Brand impersonation copies the trusted brand identity.

questions.q: An attacker registers a domain that differs from a legitimate company domain by one common typo. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Typosquatting uses misspelled or lookalike domain names.
